title: A thousand cows for the wisest
hook: a king offers a thousand gold-horned cows to the wisest person in the room, and only one man dares to take them
tomorrow: Ashvala asks about death and ritual

segments.voice: Yesterday, the honey doctrine: the earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for the earth. Your line was one self in all, so all feed each other.
screen: `ONE SELF IN ALL, SO ALL FEED EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: A royal courtyard, crowded with learned priests from the Kuru and Panchala lands. In the middle, penned together, a thousand cows. On the horns of every one, the text says, gold is tied. King Janaka stands up. Honored scholars, he says, whoever among you is wisest in Brahman, drive these cows home. The room goes silent. Nobody moves. Taking the cows means claiming to be the wisest person there, and every other priest will come for you.
screen: `A THOUSAND COWS. GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.` → `WHOEVER IS WISEST, TAKE THEM.` → `NOBODY MOVES.`

segments.voice: Then Yajnavalkya turns to his own student. Samashravas, my dear, he says, drive them home. And the student does. The room explodes. How can he call himself the wisest among us? The king's own hotri priest, Ashvala, steps up. Yajnavalkya, are you really the wisest among us? And Yajnavalkya answers. We bow to the wisest. We just want the cows. It's funny, and it's sly. He claims nothing, and he'll answer any question you've got. That sets up the whole third book of the Brihadaranyaka: a day of debate. One after another, challengers step forward, one of them twice, each with the hardest question they have. Over the next ten days we'll take them one at a time. And a word about the king. Janaka of Videha appears again and again in these texts as a king hungry for teaching. Sita's father in the Ramayana is also called Janaka, king of Videha. Nobody can say for sure whether they're the same man. Now the teaching in this scene. In the Upanishads, knowing Brahman isn't settled by a title. It's tested in the open, question by question, and Hindu tradition kept that habit of scriptural debate, later called shastrartha. And the one who knows doesn't announce it. The Bhagavad Gita says how to learn from the wise: by bowing, by asking questions, and by serving. So in this tradition, asking wait, why? isn't disrespect. It's the way in.
screen: `DRIVE THEM HOME, MY DEAR.` · `WE BOW TO THE WISEST.` · `WE JUST WANT THE COWS.` · `CHALLENGERS, ONE AT A TIME.` · `BOW, ASK, SERVE.` · then, large: `WISDOM ISN'T CLAIMED; IT'S QUESTIONED.`

segments.voice: If a memory comes, recall a time you stayed quiet in a room because speaking up meant being judged: a meeting, a class, a family dinner. Don't relive it; just notice how it felt in the body. Then bring to mind Yajnavalkya's ease, we bow to the wisest, and let some of it into your shoulders as you breathe. Your questions belong in the room.
Janaka's court. Where a king asked for the brahmishtha, the one most wise in Brahman: the title nobody there dared to claim, and Yajnavalkya never quite claimed either.
Your line: wisdom isn't claimed; it's questioned. Tomorrow, the first challenger, a priest, steps up. Day three hundred seventy-one, done.

screen: `DAY 371 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ASHVALA ASKS ABOUT DEATH AND RITUAL.`

howItsDone: The debate in Janaka's court, the third book of the Brihadaranyaka, is studied in Vedanta as a series of short dialogues; Hindu tradition remembers Janaka as a model of the king who lives among riches without clinging to them.

original.note: Sanskrit brahmiṣṭha: most knowing of Brahman, the superlative Janaka used for the prize.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a contest for cows.
what it means: a king's challenge that opens a whole day of the hardest questions in the Upanishads.
what a scholar hears: Yajnavalkya never claims to be brahmiṣṭha; namo vayaṃ brahmiṣṭhāya kurmaḥ, we bow to the wisest (3.1.2). the challengers follow one by one through 3.9, Gargi twice.

chat.meaning: Yajnavalkya took the cows without claiming to be wisest, and answered every challenger; the Gita says learn from the wise by bowing, asking and serving.

Janaka.meaning: king of Videha, hungry for teaching, who offered the cows

Samashravas.meaning: Yajnavalkya's student, who drove the cows home

hotri.meaning: the priest who recites the hymns at the fire sacrifice

Ashvala.meaning: King Janaka's hotri priest, the first challenger

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.34 (learn by bowing, by questioning, by service)

notes: Gold on the horns: the text says ten pādas of gold were tied to each cow's horns; the script says only 'gold is tied'. Confirm.
Challengers counted as eight (Ashvala, Artabhaga, Bhujyu, Ushasta, Kahola, Gargi twice, Uddalaka, Shakalya). Confirm the count fits how the path presents it.
'Over the next ten days': days 372–381 cover the challengers. Adjust if the outline changes.
Janaka of the Upanishads and Sita's father: the script says nobody can say for sure they are the same; Hindu tradition sometimes identifies them. Confirm the phrasing.
